verdict.reason: Both debates follow the same arc: the Utilitarian frames pay against pain, the other two minds lean against the commute, and the Utilitarian concedes with only a thin stated cause, so neither shows clearly stronger interaction. A is somewhat better calibrated and has one genuinely reasoned reversal; B brings more distinct cost mechanisms and a more useful observable branch but overclaims. Neither advantage would decisively change what this user takes away.

comparisons.a_observation: The Stoic first calls the commute an indifferent (A.debate[2]), then revises with a named mechanism: energy drain that undermines the capacity to act well. The Utilitarian picks up that mechanism in A.debate[6].text. The Essentialist mostly repeats its position (A.debate[4], A.debate[7]).
comparisons.b_observation: The Economist adds fragility and optionality as a cost distinct from wasted time, but the Stoic and Economist mostly reinforce each other. The Utilitarian's concession (B.debate[6].text) rests on general stress rather than on a specific objection.
comparisons.why_it_matters: In neither debate does the pro-offer side get tested and then narrowed in a way that leaves the user with a sharper criterion. A's reversal is better caused, but B gives a cost category the user might not have considered.

comparisons.a_observation: Mostly moderate claims, though it ends on moralizing ('loss of your own soul') rather than a criterion.
comparisons.b_observation: Says the raise is 'likely an illusion' and that the user is 'effectively paying the company', and invokes vehicle depreciation without knowing how the user would commute or what the numbers are.
comparisons.why_it_matters: A user deciding on a real offer could be misled by B's confident claim that the raise is net negative, which the input cannot support.

comparisons.a_observation: Branches on need versus lifestyle and suggests a one-week mock commute to measure exhaustion.
comparisons.b_observation: Same need-versus-lifestyle branches, plus whether the commute time can be used (for example transit versus driving), with a trial week. B.clearer also names an open question: whether money can later buy back time.
comparisons.why_it_matters: Whether the 90 minutes are usable time is one of the most decision-relevant facts the user did not give, and B turns it into an observable condition.

verdict.best_of_a: A.debate[5].text: The Stoic's caused self-revision, from 'the commute is irrelevant' to 'it matters if it depletes the energy needed to act well', gives the user a concrete thing to test.
verdict.best_of_b: B.dependsOn: The branch on whether commute time can be productive or restorative names a key unstated fact and ties it to a one-week test.

concerns.description: Assumes the user drives (vehicle depreciation) and asserts the raise is likely illusory, with no information about commute mode or finances.

Treating traffic reliability as black-swan exposure and claiming the commute 'removes your ability to pivot' stretch Taleb's concepts beyond the book's argument without marking this as the mind's own extension.
Both debates assume a car or traffic commute ('sitting in traffic', 'in a car', 'staring at the road') although the user did not give the commute mode.
